title: Would Aliens Interfere with Human Life
guestName: Would Aliens Interfere with Human Life
tldr: Josh Szeps and Joe Rogan explore whether extraterrestrial civilizations with the capability to reach Earth would choose to actively interfere with human life
Discussion of the Fermi Paradox and the various explanations for why the universe appears silent despite the statistical likelihood of other intelligent life
Szeps introduces the Zoo Hypothesis and other non-contact frameworks that could explain apparent alien non-interference with human civilization
Examination of whether the UAP phenomena documented by credible witnesses represents a form of low-key observation rather than direct intervention
Philosophical conversation about the assumption that alien motivations would be analogous to human ones and why that assumption may be deeply flawed
Conversation closes on what our curiosity about alien interference reveals about humanity's own sense of cosmic significance and vulnerability
recap:
Josh Szeps, the Australian journalist and media personality, joins Joe Rogan for a conversation that lands on one of the most philosophically interesting questions in the alien contact discussion: if extraterrestrial life exists and has the capability to observe or visit Earth, would they choose to interact with us, or would they stand back and watch?

Szeps approaches the topic from a science communication background, which means he brings grounded skepticism about easy answers while remaining genuinely open to the strangeness of the question. Joe has his usual enthusiasm for the subject, and the two find a productive back-and-forth that goes beyond the standard UFO talking points.

The intervention question cuts in multiple directions. On one hand, if an alien civilization has the technology to reach Earth, they likely also have the capability to intervene in human affairs in ways we couldn't prevent or even detect. On the other hand, the apparent silence of the universe despite billions of years of cosmic history might suggest that advanced civilizations develop something like a non-interference norm as part of their maturation.

Szeps brings up the Fermi Paradox and the various resolutions people have proposed. The Great Filter, the Zoo Hypothesis, the idea that technological civilizations tend to destroy themselves before reaching interstellar travel, the possibility that contact simply looks different from what we expect. Joe leans into the stranger possibilities, including the idea that UAP phenomena represent some form of non-overt observation that's been ongoing.

The conversation turns to what intervention would actually look like. Szeps argues that the concept of intervention assumes aliens would have goals analogous to human motivations, which is a significant assumption. Joe pushes back with the idea that the very fact of their presence would constitute a form of influence, regardless of conscious intent.

They close with the broader philosophical implication: that the question of whether aliens would interfere says as much about what we imagine our place in the universe to be as it does about extraterrestrial behavior or intent.
